AutoARIMA.description: Stepwise-order-search ARIMA via statsforecast, fit once and rolled forward.
AutoARIMA.compute_profile: CPU only; a stepwise order search at fit time, typically seconds per case (searched on the most recent 5,000 points by default); each origin after that is one fixed-parameter `forward` pass over that origin's whole history — ~0.03s even on a 200,000-point one, the cheapest roll-forward of the classical methods here.
AutoARIMA.limitations: Non-seasonal by default (season_length=1) — a large seasonal period would explode SARIMA's search cost, so seasonal structure isn't modeled unless you pass season_length explicitly. Univariate: ignores exogenous inputs. Order and coefficients are fixed at fit time, so a structural change in the series after fit is tracked through the recursion's state, not through re-estimation.
AutoARIMA.code_snippet:
from statsforecast.models import AutoARIMA

model = AutoARIMA(season_length=1)
model.fit(train_y)                   # train_y: 1D array -- order search once

# each origin: fixed-parameter recursion over the growing history, no re-fit
y_hat = model.forward(history_y, horizon)['mean']

AutoETS.description:
Exponential smoothing state space (auto-selected) via statsforecast, fit once and
    rolled forward.
AutoETS.compute_profile: CPU only; searches over error/trend/season state combinations at fit time, typically seconds per case (searched on the most recent 5,000 points by default); each origin after that is one fixed-parameter `forward` pass over that origin's whole history — ~0.01s even on a 200,000-point one.
AutoETS.limitations: Non-seasonal by default (season_length=1), like AutoARIMA — its seasonal state grows with the period, so a large seasonal period is impractical unless you pass season_length explicitly. Univariate: ignores exogenous inputs. Spec and smoothing parameters are fixed at fit time.
AutoETS.code_snippet:
from statsforecast.models import AutoETS

model = AutoETS(season_length=1)
model.fit(train_y)                   # train_y: 1D array -- spec search once

# each origin: fixed-parameter smoothing over the growing history, no re-fit
y_hat = model.forward(history_y, horizon)['mean']

CatBoost+exo.description: Shared lag-feature pipeline; subclasses provide the sklearn regressor.
CatBoost+exo.compute_profile: CPU only; a lag+calendar feature table is built once, then the regressor fits on it directly — fast for the linear/tree models here, slower for the MLP (which also cross-validates an early-stopping split).
CatBoost+exo.limitations: Needs enough history to fill its lag windows (shortest lag 1, longest tied to the case's declared seasonal periods). The univariate variant ignores exogenous inputs entirely; the +exo variant sees only the future covariate values supplied at predict time (a perfect-forecast proxy in this benchmark, not a real forecast of those covariates).
CatBoost+exo.code_snippet:
from mlforecast import MLForecast

fcst = MLForecast(
    models=[<regressor>],           # e.g. LGBMRegressor, Ridge, MLPRegressor
    freq=case.freq,
    lags=[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, *case.seasonalities],
    date_features=["dayofweek", "month", ...],
)
fcst.fit(train_df, static_features=[])
y_hat = fcst.predict(h=horizon, ids=[target_uid])

Chronos-2+exo.compute_profile: CPU-capable but slower than Chronos-Bolt (120M params); zero-shot, so there's no per-case training — one forward pass per prediction via the DataFrame API. The pretrained model is loaded once and cached across every case and origin.
Chronos-2+exo.limitations: Zero-shot: never learns anything case-specific, only what it picked up from pretraining on other series. Univariate by default — Chronos-2 supports covariates natively, and the +exo variant feeds the case's declared covariates to `predict_df` as past+future covariate columns, using a perfect-forecast proxy (not a real forecast of those covariates) for the future values. Conditions on a fixed window sized to the case's pre-test history, capped at `context_length` points.
Chronos-2+exo.code_snippet:
from chronos import Chronos2Pipeline

pipe = Chronos2Pipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cpu")
pred = pipe.predict_df(
    context_df,                      # id / timestamp / target (+ covariate) columns
    future_df=future_df,             # +exo: future covariate values (id/timestamp/cols)
    prediction_length=horizon,
    quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9],
    id_column="id",
    timestamp_column="timestamp",
    target="target",
)
y_hat = pred["predictions"]          # median

Climatology.description:
Mean target value by position within the case's dominant declared seasonal cycle
    (`case.seasonalities`). Keying on the declared seasonality means the baseline has the
    same meaning at every frequency, rather than shifting between day-of-year, hour, and
    weekday x hour depending on the sampling rate. A non-seasonal case (`seasonalities =
    []`) has no cycle to key on, so every timestamp shares one bucket and the baseline is
    the global training mean. A stronger 'no-skill' reference than Mean for series with a
    stable seasonal/diurnal cycle.
Climatology.compute_profile: CPU, negligible — one groupby-mean over the training split.
Climatology.limitations: Averages history by position in the dominant seasonal cycle, so it captures a stable average shape but not trend, one-off events, or year-to-year drift; falls back to the global mean on a case declared non-seasonal.
Climatology.code_snippet:
position = position_in_cycle(freq, period, train['ds'])
climatology = train.groupby(position)['y'].mean()
y_hat = [climatology[position_in_cycle(freq, period, ds)] for ds in future_ds]

DLinear.compute_profile: CPU only, fast; both linear maps collapse into a single closed-form ridge fit on the decomposed window, so there's no gradient-descent training loop.
DLinear.limitations: Univariate — ignores exogenous inputs. The trend/remainder decomposition is a fixed moving average, not learned, so an unusually shaped trend can leak into the remainder term.
DLinear.code_snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

trend = moving_average(window, kernel)
remainder = window - trend
model = Ridge(alpha=alpha).fit(concat([trend, remainder]), target_window)
y_hat = model.predict(concat([trend, remainder]))

iTransformer.description: Shared neuralforecast wrapper; subclasses name the model class + extra kwargs.
iTransformer.compute_profile: Uses a GPU automatically if one is available (accelerator='auto'), otherwise falls back to CPU; a heavier training loop (up to 500 steps, full pytorch_lightning trainer overhead) than the custom torch models in torchdl.py. Only available on Linux with Python <3.13 (the `nf` extra), since neuralforecast depends on `ray`.
iTransformer.limitations: Univariate — ignores exogenous inputs. Trains a fresh model per case with no hyperparameter tuning, using the same architecture defaults regardless of the series' scale or frequency. Architecturally multivariate but fixed to a single series here (n_series=1), so unlike its siblings it can't pool the extra segments of an extended-history fit.
iTransformer.code_snippet:
import neuralforecast.models as nfm
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast

model = getattr(nfm, model_name)(h=horizon, input_size=lookback, max_steps=500)
nf = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq=case.freq)
nf.fit(train_df)                     # train_df: unique_id, ds, y
y_hat = nf.predict()[model_name]

MSTL-ARIMA.description:
MSTL with an AutoARIMA trend-cycle/residual forecaster. Capped tighter than
    MSTL-ETS because the ARIMA stepwise search is the more expensive fit.
MSTL-ARIMA.compute_profile: CPU only; a fast STL-based decomposition plus the subclass's trend forecaster, on the most recent 8,000 points — typically seconds per case. Each origin after that re-derives STL over that origin's whole history and forwards the trend model with its parameters fixed; STL cost grows with history x period, so a long record is slow — ~0.7s at 5,000 points up to ~28s at 200,000 for periods [24, 168].
MSTL-ARIMA.limitations: Univariate: ignores exogenous inputs. Needs at least 2 full cycles of each declared seasonal period in the training window to fit at all; raises rather than degenerating into a duplicate non-seasonal forecast when a case has no seasonality it can use. The trend model's parameters are fixed at fit time; the STL decomposition around them is re-derived from each origin's full history, which keeps the seasonal shape current but makes predict the expensive half on a long record.
MSTL-ARIMA.code_snippet:
from statsforecast.models import MSTL

model = MSTL(season_length=periods, trend_forecaster=<trend_forecaster>)
model.fit(train_y)                   # train_y: 1D array -- decompose + fit once

# each origin: re-derive STL, forward the fixed-parameter trend model, reseasonalize
y_hat = model.forward(history_y, horizon)['mean']

Mean.compute_profile: CPU, negligible — one mean over the training split.
Mean.limitations: Ignores trend, seasonality, and recency entirely; useful only as a floor other methods should comfortably beat.

Moirai-2.0+exo.compute_profile: CPU-capable but slow; zero-shot, so there's no per-case training — one forward pass per prediction through the GluonTS predictor. The pretrained weights are loaded once and cached across every case and origin.
Moirai-2.0+exo.limitations: Zero-shot: never learns anything case-specific, only what it picked up from pretraining on other series. Univariate by default — Moirai supports covariates natively, and the +exo variant feeds the case's declared covariates in as `feat_dynamic_real`, using a perfect-forecast proxy (not a real forecast of those covariates) for the future values. N-HiTS.compute_profile: CPU (no GPU dependency); trains a small network from scratch per case — 600 gradient steps over randomly sampled windows — making these the heaviest CPU methods in the benchmark. Keep rolling-origin counts modest when including them.
N-HiTS.limitations: Univariate — ignores exogenous inputs (the covariate story lives in the windowed-ML +exo columns instead). Each window is instance-normalised (RevIN-style) before the model and de-normalised after, which is what makes the same architecture usable across very different series scales.
N-HiTS.code_snippet:
net = <NHiTSNet or PatchTSTNet>(lookback, horizon)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for step in range(600):
    xb, yb = sample_batch(windows, batch_size=256)
    mu, sd = xb.mean(1), xb.std(1)          # per-window instance norm
    pred = net((xb - mu) / sd) * sd + mu
    loss = mse_loss(pred, yb)
    loss.backward(); opt.step()

PatchTST.compute_profile: CPU (no GPU dependency); trains a small network from scratch per case — 600 gradient steps over randomly sampled windows — making these the heaviest CPU methods in the benchmark. Keep rolling-origin counts modest when including them.
PatchTST.limitations: Univariate — ignores exogenous inputs (the covariate story lives in the windowed-ML +exo columns instead). Each window is instance-normalised (RevIN-style) before the model and de-normalised after, which is what makes the same architecture usable across very different series scales.
PatchTST.code_snippet:
net = <NHiTSNet or PatchTSTNet>(lookback, horizon)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for step in range(600):
    xb, yb = sample_batch(windows, batch_size=256)
    mu, sd = xb.mean(1), xb.std(1)          # per-window instance norm
    pred = net((xb - mu) / sd) * sd + mu
    loss = mse_loss(pred, yb)
    loss.backward(); opt.step()

Persistence.compute_profile: CPU, negligible — no fitting at all.
Persistence.limitations: Repeats the last observed value for the whole horizon; degrades fast on any series with a trend, cycle, or fast dynamics beyond one step.

SeasonalNaive.compute_profile: CPU, negligible — tiles the last observed seasonal cycle.
SeasonalNaive.limitations: Repeats the most recent full cycle of the case's dominant declared seasonal period; refuses to run on a case declared non-seasonal, and can't adapt if the cycle's shape drifts over time.

TBATS.description:
TBATS (Trigonometric, Box-Cox, ARMA, Trend, Seasonal) via statsforecast, fit once
    and rolled forward.
TBATS.compute_profile: CPU only; a genuine AIC search over Box-Cox/trend/damped-trend/ARMA-error combinations at fit time (up to 12 candidate models) -- the heaviest single fit of the classical methods here, on the order of a minute at 3,000 points with an annual (365) season. Paid once, though: each origin after that is a fixed-coefficient state-space filter pass (`calcTBATSFaster`) over that origin's whole history, on the order of milliseconds even on long records.
TBATS.limitations: Univariate: ignores exogenous inputs. Its internal Box-Cox transform assumes strictly positive data; a Yeo-Johnson fallback (see below) handles series that dip to zero or negative. The roll-forward calls two statsforecast internals (`calcTBATSFaster`, `tbats_forecast`) directly rather than a public `forward()` method, since none exists for TBATS -- pinned bit-exact against `AutoTBATS`'s own output (see the class docstring), but a soft dependency on library internals that could break on a future statsforecast version bump.
TBATS.code_snippet:
from statsforecast.tbats import tbats_selection, calcTBATSFaster, tbats_forecast

# fit once: genuine AIC search over Box-Cox/trend/damped-trend/ARMA-errors
mod = tbats_selection(train_y, [season_length], use_boxcox=None, use_trend=None,
                      use_damped_trend=None, use_arma_errors=True, ...)

# each origin: roll the frozen coefficients forward over the growing history
_, _, x = calcTBATSFaster(history_y, mod['w_transpose'], mod['g'], mod['F'],
                          mod['seed_states'])
y_hat = tbats_forecast({'x': x, 'w_transpose': mod['w_transpose'], 'F': mod['F']},
                       horizon)['mean']

Only available on Linux with Python <3.13 (the `nf` extra), since neuralforecast depends on `ray`.

nf = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq=case.freq)
nf.fit(train_df)                     # train_df: unique_id, ds, y
y_hat = nf.predict()[model_name]

Theta.description:
Theta method (auto-optimized) via statsforecast — a strong, cheap classical
    benchmark, often the one to beat among non-ML methods.
Theta.compute_profile: CPU only; a cheap deseasonalize/fit/re-seasonalize decomposition at fit time (searched on the most recent 8,000 points). Cheap to fit, but the most expensive roll-forward here: each origin re-derives the decomposition and re-runs the fixed-parameter filter over that origin's whole history, at a cost superlinear in its length — 0.02s at 5,000 points, ~2.5s at 50,000, ~110s at 200,000.
Theta.limitations: Univariate: ignores exogenous inputs. Parameters are fixed at fit time, but the deseasonalization is a fixed classical decomposition re-derived from each origin's history rather than a learned model, so it can lag a genuinely shifting seasonal shape and its multiplicative-vs-additive choice can differ between origins.
Theta.code_snippet:
from statsforecast.models import AutoTheta

model = AutoTheta(season_length=season_length)
model.fit(train_y)                   # train_y: 1D array -- picks params once

# each origin: fixed-parameter filter over the growing history, no re-fit
y_hat = model.forward(history_y, horizon)['mean']

TimesFM-2.5+exo.compute_profile: CPU-capable but slow (200M params); zero-shot, so there's no per-case training — one forward pass per prediction. The pretrained weights are loaded once per process; each distinct per-case context length gets its own cheap compiled variant (a shallow copy of the loaded model, not a reload), cached across every origin of that case.
TimesFM-2.5+exo.limitations: Zero-shot: never learns anything case-specific, only what it picked up from pretraining. Univariate by default — the +exo variant feeds the case's declared covariates to `forecast_with_covariates` as an xreg regressor fit alongside the TimesFM forecast, using a perfect-forecast proxy (not a real forecast of those covariates) for the future values. Conditions on a fixed window sized to the case's pre-test history, capped at the checkpoint's `context_limit`; horizons beyond `max_horizon` are not supported.
TimesFM-2.5+exo.code_snippet:
import timesfm

model = timesfm.TimesFM_2p5_200M_torch.from_pretrained("google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch")
model.compile(timesfm.ForecastConfig(max_context=1024, max_horizon=256,
    normalize_inputs=True, use_continuous_quantile_head=True))
point_forecast, _quantiles = model.forecast(
    horizon=horizon,
    inputs=[context],                # list of 1D arrays, one per series
)
y_hat = point_forecast[0]
# +exo: model.forecast_with_covariates(inputs=[context],
#     dynamic_numerical_covariates={name: [context_and_horizon_values]})

TimesNet.description: Shared neuralforecast wrapper; subclasses name the model class + extra kwargs.
TimesNet.compute_profile: Uses a GPU automatically if one is available (accelerator='auto'), otherwise falls back to CPU; a heavier training loop (up to 500 steps, full pytorch_lightning trainer overhead) than the custom torch models in torchdl.py. Only available on Linux with Python <3.13 (the `nf` extra), since neuralforecast depends on `ray`.
TimesNet.limitations: Univariate — ignores exogenous inputs. Trains a fresh model per case with no hyperparameter tuning, using the same architecture defaults regardless of the series' scale or frequency.
TimesNet.code_snippet:
import neuralforecast.models as nfm
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast

model = getattr(nfm, model_name)(h=horizon, input_size=lookback, max_steps=500)
nf = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq=case.freq)
nf.fit(train_df)                     # train_df: unique_id, ds, y
y_hat = nf.predict()[model_name]

EnsembleBaselines.description: Combine several member forecasters into one via a per-step median (or mean).
EnsembleBaselines.library: no additional library — combines member forecasters' own outputs
EnsembleBaselines.compute_profile: Sum of its members' costs; cheap in practice since the members are the naive baselines (and optionally the fast classical Theta method).
EnsembleBaselines.limitations: Only as good as its members — a median/mean of weak forecasts is still weak. A member that fails at one origin is silently dropped from that step's combination rather than failing the whole prediction.
EnsembleBaselines.code_snippet:
member_forecasts = [m.predict(case, history, horizon) for m in members]
stacked = np.vstack([f['y_hat'] for f in member_forecasts])
y_hat = np.nanmedian(stacked, axis=0)   # or np.nanmean if combine='mean'
